skills.title: Independent Variables
skills.summary: The independent variable is the one factor the investigator deliberately changes to see what effect it has. A well-designed experiment changes only one independent variable at a time.
objectives: Identify the independent variable in an investigation.
Explain why it is deliberately changed.
Recognize that only one should change at a time.

skills.title: Dependent Variables
skills.summary: The dependent variable is the outcome the investigator measures to see whether changing the independent variable had an effect. Its value depends on what was changed, which is why it is measured rather than set.
objectives: Identify the dependent variable in an investigation.
Distinguish it from the independent variable.
Explain why it is measured, not chosen.

skills.title: Controlled Variables
skills.summary: Controlled variables are the factors deliberately kept the same for every trial so they cannot affect the result. Holding them constant is what allows a difference in the outcome to be attributed to the independent variable.
objectives: Identify controlled variables in an investigation.
Explain why they are held constant.
Spot an uncontrolled factor that would spoil a test.

skills.title: Control Groups
skills.summary: A control group is a set of trials that does not receive the treatment being tested, providing a baseline for comparison. Without it there is nothing to judge the treated group against.
objectives: Explain the purpose of a control group.
Identify the control group in an investigation.
Recognize when a study lacks one.

skills.title: Repeated Trials
skills.summary: Repeating an experiment several times and comparing the results reveals random variation and makes the findings more reliable. A single trial can be misleading, so results are usually averaged across trials.
objectives: Explain why experiments are repeated.
Compute a mean across trials.
Recognize an unreliable single-trial result.

skills.title: Fair Tests
skills.summary: A fair test changes only the independent variable while holding every other relevant factor constant, so the comparison is valid. If more than one factor differs, the test is not fair and no cause can be identified.
objectives: Judge whether an investigation is a fair test.
Explain what makes a test fair.
Correct an unfair test.

skills.title: Sources of Error
skills.summary: Experimental error is the difference between a measured value and the true value. Random errors vary unpredictably between trials and are reduced by repeating and averaging, while systematic errors shift every reading the same way and must be corrected at the source.
objectives: Distinguish random from systematic error.
Identify likely sources of error in a procedure.
Choose an appropriate way to reduce a given error.

components.body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to identify the independent variable in an investigation.
Recall that a hypothesis proposes a testable relationship, usually of the form 'if this changes, then that will happen'.

To find out whether more light makes a plant grow taller, you decide how much light each plant gets. Light is the thing you set on purpose, so it is the independent variable. If you also changed the water, you could not tell which change caused any difference.

The independent variable is the factor the investigator deliberately changes or selects in order to test its effect. To keep results interpretable, only one independent variable is changed in an experiment.
In a test of how fertilizer amount affects plant height, plants get 0 g, 5 g, or 10 g of fertilizer. The amount of fertilizer is chosen by the investigator, so it is the independent variable.
You test whether water temperature affects how fast sugar dissolves. The independent variable is the water temperature, because you set it.
A common mistake is confusing the independent variable with the result you measure. The independent variable is what you change; the result is what you observe.
The independent variable is the single factor you deliberately change to test its effect. Changing only one at a time keeps the results interpretable.
In an experiment on how light affects plant growth, which variable is independent, and why?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to identify the dependent variable and distinguish it from the independent variable.
Recall that the independent variable is the factor you deliberately change.

If you change how much light plants get, the thing you then measure is how tall they grow. You do not decide the height; it comes out of the experiment. Because it depends on the light, it is the dependent variable.
The dependent variable is the outcome measured in an experiment. Its value depends on the independent variable, so it is recorded rather than set by the investigator.
In a study of how fertilizer amount affects plant height, height is measured at the end. Height is the dependent variable because it responds to the fertilizer.
You change water temperature and record how long sugar takes to dissolve. The dissolving time is the dependent variable, because you measure it.
A common mistake is swapping the two variables. Ask: did I set this value (independent) or did I measure it at the end (dependent)?
The dependent variable is the measured outcome whose value depends on the independent variable. You record it rather than choose it.
How can you tell the dependent variable from the independent variable?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to identify controlled variables and explain their role.
Recall the independent variable (what you change) and the dependent variable (what you measure).

Testing whether light affects plant growth, you give every plant the same water, the same soil, and the same pot size. If one plant also got extra water, you could not say whether light or water caused it to grow taller. Keeping everything else the same isolates the factor you are testing.

Controlled variables are all the factors deliberately held constant across every trial so they do not influence the dependent variable. Controlling them is what allows a causal link between the independent and dependent variables.
In a light-and-plant-growth test, controlled variables include the amount of water, the soil type, the pot size, and the temperature. Only the light differs between plants.
You test how slope steepness affects rolling distance. Controlled variables include using the same ball and the same floor surface each time.
A common mistake is letting a second factor vary along with the independent variable. If two things change together, the results cannot show which one caused the effect.
Controlled variables are held constant across trials so only the independent variable differs. Controlling them is what makes the comparison fair and the conclusion valid.
Why must factors other than the independent variable be kept the same?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to identify a control group and explain why it is needed.
Recall controlled variables, which are kept the same across trials. A control group takes this further by omitting the treatment entirely.

If every plant gets fertilizer and they all grow, you cannot say the fertilizer helped, because you do not know how they would have grown without it. Keeping some plants fertilizer-free gives you that comparison.
A control group is the group that does not receive the treatment or experimental condition, while the experimental group does. Comparing the two shows what difference the treatment actually made.

Testing a fertilizer, one set of plants gets fertilizer (experimental group) and an otherwise identical set gets none (control group). If the fertilized plants grow taller, the difference can be credited to the fertilizer.
In a medicine trial, the group receiving no medicine (or a placebo) is the control group; it shows what happens without treatment.
A common mistake is treating every subject and having no baseline. Without a control group, you cannot know whether the observed change was caused by the treatment.
A control group receives no treatment and provides the baseline for comparison. Without one, an experiment cannot show that the treatment caused the result.
Why is an experiment weaker if every group receives the treatment?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain why trials are repeated and to average results across them.
Recall that measurements carry error, and that controlled variables keep conditions the same between trials.

Timing the same rolling ball three times gives slightly different values, because tiny differences and reaction time creep in. One trial could be unusually fast by chance. Repeating and averaging smooths out that randomness.

Repeated trials are multiple runs of the same procedure under the same conditions. They expose random variation, improve reliability, and are usually summarized with a mean (the sum of the values divided by how many there are).
Three trials give 12 cm, 14 cm, and 13 cm. The mean is (12 + 14 + 13) divided by 3 = 39 / 3 = 13 cm.
Trials of 8 s, 10 s, and 9 s give a mean of 27 / 3 = 9 s.
A common mistake is drawing a firm conclusion from a single trial. One result may be an outlier caused by chance, so repetition is needed.
Repeating trials reveals random variation and makes results more reliable. Results across trials are typically averaged using the mean.
Why is a conclusion based on a single trial unreliable?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to judge whether a test is fair and to fix one that is not.
Recall independent, dependent, and controlled variables. A fair test is what you get when those roles are respected.

Comparing two paper airplanes to see which design flies farther, you must throw both with the same force, from the same height, in the same room. If you throw one harder, the test tells you nothing about the designs.

A fair test changes only the independent variable and holds all other relevant factors constant, so that any difference in the dependent variable can be attributed to the change. If two or more factors differ, the test is unfair and inconclusive.

Two plants are compared for light. One is in a sunny window and one in a dark cupboard, but the cupboard plant is also watered less. This is not a fair test: light and water both differ. Give both the same water to make it fair.
To compare two ramps fairly, use the same ball, released from the same starting point, on the same surface, changing only the ramp.
A common mistake is changing the setup for convenience mid-experiment, such as switching to a different measuring instrument, which quietly makes the test unfair.
A fair test changes one factor and keeps everything else the same, so the result can be trusted to reflect that factor.
What single rule makes an investigation a fair test?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to identify sources of error and choose ways to reduce them.
Recall accuracy (closeness to the true value) and precision (consistency between trials), and that trials are repeated to expose variation.

If your hand wobbles on a stopwatch, sometimes you press early and sometimes late; averaging many trials cancels much of that out. But if the balance reads 2 g too high every single time, averaging will not help at all, because every reading is shifted the same way. Those are two different kinds of error.

Random error varies unpredictably between measurements and is reduced by repeating trials and averaging. Systematic error shifts every measurement in the same direction, often from a mis-calibrated instrument or a flawed procedure, and is corrected by fixing or recalibrating the source, not by averaging.
A balance is not zeroed and reads 2 g high on every sample. This is a systematic error: all readings are too large by the same amount. Averaging cannot fix it; the balance must be re-zeroed.
Hand-timing gives 10.2, 10.4, and 10.0 seconds. The scatter comes from reaction time, a random error, best reduced by repeating trials and averaging.
A common mistake is assuming that taking more readings fixes every error. Repetition reduces random error only; a systematic error persists no matter how many times you measure.
Random errors scatter unpredictably and are reduced by repeating and averaging; systematic errors shift all readings the same way and must be corrected at the source.
Why does averaging more trials fail to remove a systematic error?

questions.prompt: In an experiment testing how light affects plant growth, what is the independent variable?

answer_spec.correct_answer: the amount of light

hints.text: It is the factor you set on purpose.
You choose how much light each plant gets.

questions.explanation: The amount of light is deliberately changed by the investigator, so it is the independent variable.

questions.prompt: The independent variable is best described as the one that is what?

answer_spec.correct_answer: deliberately changed by the investigator

hints.text: Think about who decides its value.

questions.explanation: The independent variable is the factor the investigator deliberately changes.

questions.prompt: Plants receive 0 g, 5 g, or 10 g of fertilizer, and their heights are recorded. What is the independent variable?

answer_spec.correct_answer: the amount of fertilizer

hints.text: Which factor was set at different levels on purpose?

questions.explanation: The fertilizer amount is set by the investigator, making it the independent variable.

questions.prompt: Why should only one independent variable change in an experiment?

answer_spec.correct_answer: so any effect can be traced to that one factor

hints.text: Two changes at once confuse the cause.
One change keeps the cause clear.

questions.explanation: Changing one factor at a time lets you attribute any observed effect to that factor.

options: so any effect can be traced to that one factor
because more variables are impossible to measure
so the hypothesis is always supported

questions.prompt: You test whether water temperature affects how fast sugar dissolves. What is the independent variable?

answer_spec.correct_answer: the water temperature

hints.text: You choose the temperatures to test.

questions.explanation: The water temperature is chosen by the investigator, so it is the independent variable.

questions.prompt: An experiment changes both the light and the water given to plants. What is the problem?

answer_spec.correct_answer: you cannot tell which change caused the effect

questions.explanation: With two factors changing, any difference cannot be attributed to one of them.

options: you cannot tell which change caused the effect

questions.prompt: In a hypothesis 'if the slope is steeper, then the ball rolls farther', which is the independent variable?

answer_spec.correct_answer: the steepness of the slope

hints.text: The 'if' part names what you change.

questions.explanation: The 'if' clause names the independent variable: the steepness of the slope.

questions.prompt: Which question could an independent variable answer?

answer_spec.correct_answer: What did I change on purpose?

hints.text: The independent variable is chosen by the investigator.

questions.explanation: The independent variable answers 'what did I deliberately change?'.

options: What did I change on purpose?

questions.prompt: In an experiment testing how light affects plant growth, what is the dependent variable?

answer_spec.correct_answer: the height of the plant

hints.text: It is the outcome you measure.
Plant height is recorded at the end.

questions.explanation: Plant height is measured as the outcome, so it is the dependent variable.

questions.prompt: The dependent variable is the one that is what?

answer_spec.correct_answer: measured as the outcome

hints.text: You do not choose its value.

questions.explanation: The dependent variable is measured as the outcome of the experiment.

questions.prompt: You change water temperature and record how long sugar takes to dissolve. What is the dependent variable?

answer_spec.correct_answer: the dissolving time

hints.text: What did you measure at the end?
The time was recorded, not chosen.

questions.explanation: The dissolving time is measured, making it the dependent variable.

questions.prompt: Why is it called the 'dependent' variable?

answer_spec.correct_answer: because its value depends on the independent variable

hints.text: Its value follows from what you changed.
It depends on the independent variable.

questions.explanation: It is called dependent because its value depends on the factor that was changed.

options: because its value depends on the independent variable
because it depends on the weather

questions.prompt: In 'if the slope is steeper, then the ball rolls farther', which is the dependent variable?

answer_spec.correct_answer: the distance the ball rolls

questions.explanation: The 'then' clause names the dependent variable: the distance the ball rolls.

questions.prompt: Which question does the dependent variable answer?

answer_spec.correct_answer: What did I measure?

questions.explanation: The dependent variable answers 'what did I measure?'.

questions.prompt: A student sets three light levels and measures leaf count. Which pair is correct?

answer_spec.correct_answer: independent: light level; dependent: leaf count

hints.text: The set factor is independent; the measured one is dependent.
Light was set, leaves were counted.

questions.explanation: Light level was deliberately set (independent) and leaf count was measured (dependent).

options: independent: light level; dependent: leaf count
independent: leaf count; dependent: light level

common_wrong_answers.value: independent: leaf count; dependent: light level

questions.prompt: On a results graph, the dependent variable is usually plotted on which axis?

answer_spec.correct_answer: the vertical (y) axis

hints.text: The measured outcome goes up the side.

questions.explanation: By convention the measured dependent variable is plotted on the vertical y-axis.

questions.prompt: Controlled variables are the factors that are what?

answer_spec.correct_answer: kept the same in every trial

questions.explanation: Controlled variables are deliberately kept constant across all trials.

options: kept the same in every trial

questions.prompt: In a test of how light affects plant growth, which is a controlled variable?

answer_spec.correct_answer: the amount of water each plant receives

hints.text: It must be identical for every plant.

questions.explanation: Water is kept the same for every plant so only light differs.

options: the amount of water each plant receives

questions.prompt: Why are controlled variables kept constant?

answer_spec.correct_answer: so the result can be attributed to the independent variable

hints.text: Constant factors cannot explain a difference.

questions.explanation: Holding other factors constant means any difference in the outcome must come from the independent variable.

options: so the result can be attributed to the independent variable
to increase the number of variables

questions.prompt: In a light-and-plant-growth experiment, select every controlled variable.

hints.text: Light is changed and height is measured; the rest are held constant.

questions.explanation: Soil type, pot size, and water amount are held constant; light is the independent variable and height the dependent one.

questions.prompt: One plant in a light experiment accidentally gets extra water. What has happened?

answer_spec.correct_answer: a controlled variable was not held constant, so the result is unreliable

hints.text: Water should have been the same for all.
An uncontrolled factor spoils the comparison.

questions.explanation: Water was supposed to be controlled; letting it vary means the outcome cannot be attributed to light alone.

options: a controlled variable was not held constant, so the result is unreliable

questions.prompt: In a test of how slope steepness affects rolling distance, which should be controlled?

answer_spec.correct_answer: the ball used each time

hints.text: Use the same ball for every trial.

questions.explanation: Using the same ball each time controls a factor that could otherwise affect distance.

questions.prompt: Which question do controlled variables answer?

answer_spec.correct_answer: What did I keep the same?

hints.text: They answer what stayed the same.

questions.explanation: Controlled variables answer 'what did I keep the same?'.

options: What did I keep the same?

questions.prompt: An experiment has no controlled variables. What can you conclude from it?

answer_spec.correct_answer: very little, because any factor could have caused the result

hints.text: Many things could differ between trials.

questions.explanation: Without controls, any of several factors could explain the outcome, so no firm conclusion is possible.

options: very little, because any factor could have caused the result
the exact cause of the effect

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a control group?

answer_spec.correct_answer: to provide a baseline for comparison

hints.text: It shows what happens without the treatment.

questions.explanation: The control group shows what happens without the treatment, giving a baseline to compare against.

options: to provide a baseline for comparison

questions.prompt: In a fertilizer test, which set of plants is the control group?

answer_spec.correct_answer: the plants that receive no fertilizer

hints.text: The control does not get the treatment.

questions.explanation: The plants receiving no fertilizer form the control group.

options: the plants that receive no fertilizer
the plants that receive the most fertilizer

questions.prompt: Every plant in a study receives fertilizer and they all grow. What is the flaw?

answer_spec.correct_answer: there is no control group, so the growth cannot be credited to the fertilizer

hints.text: Nothing shows what would happen without it.

questions.explanation: Without an untreated control group, the growth might have happened anyway, so the fertilizer cannot be credited.

options: there is no control group, so the growth cannot be credited to the fertilizer

questions.prompt: In a medicine trial, what does the control group receive?

answer_spec.correct_answer: no medicine, or a placebo

hints.text: The control does not get the real treatment.
It gets nothing or a placebo.

questions.explanation: The control group receives no active medicine, often a placebo, to provide a baseline.

questions.prompt: The group that does receive the treatment is called the what?

answer_spec.correct_answer: experimental group

hints.text: It is the opposite of the control group.

questions.explanation: The group receiving the treatment is the experimental group.

questions.prompt: Apart from the treatment, how should the control group compare to the experimental group?

answer_spec.correct_answer: as similar as possible in every other way

questions.explanation: The two groups should be alike in every respect except the treatment, so only it can explain a difference.

options: as similar as possible in every other way

questions.prompt: The control plants grew just as tall as the fertilized plants. What does this suggest?

answer_spec.correct_answer: the fertilizer had little or no effect

hints.text: No difference means no detectable effect.

questions.explanation: If both groups grew the same, the fertilizer made no measurable difference.

options: the fertilizer had little or no effect

questions.prompt: A control group is most useful because it answers which question?

answer_spec.correct_answer: What would have happened without the treatment?

hints.text: It shows the outcome without treatment.

questions.explanation: The control group answers what would have happened without the treatment.

options: What would have happened without the treatment?

questions.prompt: Why are experiments repeated several times?

answer_spec.correct_answer: to reveal random variation and make results more reliable

hints.text: A single result can be a fluke.

questions.explanation: Repeating trials shows random variation and makes conclusions more reliable.

options: to reveal random variation and make results more reliable

questions.prompt: Three trials give 12 cm, 14 cm, and 13 cm. What is the mean, in centimeters?

hints.text: Add the values, then divide by 3.

questions.explanation: The mean is (12 + 14 + 13) / 3 = 13 cm.

questions.prompt: Three timed trials give 8 s, 10 s, and 9 s. What is the mean, in seconds?
questions.explanation: The mean is (8 + 10 + 9) / 3 = 9 s.

questions.prompt: A student runs one trial and draws a firm conclusion. What is the problem?

answer_spec.correct_answer: a single trial may be unusual by chance

hints.text: One result might be a fluke.

questions.explanation: One trial can be an outlier produced by chance, so it cannot support a firm conclusion.

options: a single trial may be unusual by chance

questions.prompt: Four trials give 20, 22, 21, and 21 grams. What is the mean, in grams?

hints.text: Add all four, then divide by 4.

questions.prompt: Repeated trials give widely differing results. What does this suggest?

answer_spec.correct_answer: the measurement has low reliability

questions.explanation: A wide spread across trials indicates the measurement or procedure is not reliable.

questions.prompt: What is the mean of a set of trial results?

answer_spec.correct_answer: the sum divided by the number of trials

questions.explanation: The mean is the sum of the values divided by how many there are.

options: the sum divided by the number of trials
the difference between the largest and smallest

questions.prompt: Five trials give 5, 6, 5, 7, and 7 seconds. What is the mean, in seconds?

hints.text: Add all five, then divide by 5.

questions.prompt: What makes an investigation a fair test?

answer_spec.correct_answer: only the independent variable changes; everything else is kept the same

questions.explanation: A fair test changes only the independent variable and holds all other relevant factors constant.

options: only the independent variable changes; everything else is kept the same

questions.prompt: One plant sits in sunlight and another in a cupboard, but the cupboard plant is also watered less. Is this a fair test of light?

answer_spec.correct_answer: No, because water also differs

questions.explanation: Both light and water differ, so any growth difference cannot be attributed to light alone.

options: Yes, because light is the main factor

questions.prompt: How would you fix the test above?

answer_spec.correct_answer: give both plants the same amount of water

questions.explanation: Giving both plants identical water leaves light as the only difference, making the test fair.

options: give both plants the same amount of water
put both plants in the cupboard

questions.prompt: To compare two ramp designs fairly, what should stay the same?

answer_spec.correct_answer: the ball and its release point

hints.text: Use the same ball, released the same way.

questions.explanation: Using the same ball and release point ensures only the ramp design differs.

options: the ball and its release point

questions.prompt: Two paper airplanes are compared, but one is thrown much harder. What is wrong?

answer_spec.correct_answer: throwing force differs, so the designs cannot be compared

questions.explanation: Because throwing force differs as well as the design, the comparison is unfair and inconclusive.

options: throwing force differs, so the designs cannot be compared

questions.prompt: A student switches to a different ruler halfway through an experiment. Why is this a problem?

answer_spec.correct_answer: it introduces a second change, making the test unfair

hints.text: The measuring method should stay constant.

questions.explanation: Changing instruments mid-experiment introduces a second variable, undermining the fairness of the test.

options: it introduces a second change, making the test unfair

questions.prompt: In a fair test, how many independent variables change?

answer_spec.correct_answer: one

questions.explanation: A fair test changes exactly one independent variable.

questions.prompt: Why does an unfair test give an inconclusive result?

answer_spec.correct_answer: because the effect cannot be traced to a single factor

questions.explanation: When several factors differ, no single one can be identified as the cause, so the result is inconclusive.

options: because the effect cannot be traced to a single factor
because the data is always wrong

questions.prompt: A balance is not zeroed and reads 2 g high every time. What kind of error is this?

answer_spec.correct_answer: systematic error

hints.text: Every reading is shifted the same way.

questions.explanation: A consistent shift in one direction on every reading is a systematic error.

questions.prompt: Hand-timing gives 10.2, 10.4, and 10.0 seconds. What kind of error causes this scatter?

answer_spec.correct_answer: random error

questions.explanation: Reaction-time variation scatters readings unpredictably, which is random error.

questions.prompt: How is random error best reduced?

answer_spec.correct_answer: by repeating trials and averaging

hints.text: Randomness cancels out over many trials.

questions.explanation: Repeating trials and averaging reduces random error because the variations tend to cancel.

questions.prompt: How is systematic error best reduced?

answer_spec.correct_answer: by finding and correcting its cause, such as recalibrating the instrument

hints.text: Fix the source of the shift.

questions.explanation: A systematic error must be corrected at its source, for example by recalibrating the instrument.

options: by finding and correcting its cause, such as recalibrating the instrument

questions.prompt: Why does averaging more trials not remove a systematic error?

answer_spec.correct_answer: because every reading is shifted the same way

hints.text: All readings are off in the same direction.

questions.explanation: Because a systematic error shifts every reading identically, averaging preserves the shift.

options: because every reading is shifted the same way
because the trials are too few

questions.prompt: A thermometer is always read from above eye level, giving a slightly high value each time. What error is this?

answer_spec.correct_answer: systematic error

hints.text: The same mistake occurs every reading.

questions.explanation: A consistent viewing mistake biases every reading the same way, which is systematic error.

questions.prompt: What is experimental error?

answer_spec.correct_answer: the difference between a measured value and the true value

hints.text: It is about measurement, not mistakes in general.
It is the gap from the true value.

questions.explanation: Experimental error is the difference between what was measured and the true value.

options: the difference between a measured value and the true value

questions.prompt: Select every likely source of random error in a hand-timed experiment.

correct_answer: reaction time when starting the stopwatch

hints.text: Random errors vary from trial to trial.
A mis-calibrated instrument is systematic, not random.

questions.explanation: Reaction time and small release differences vary unpredictably (random); an uncalibrated balance and a consistently mis-read scale are systematic.

options: reaction time when starting the stopwatch
always reading the scale from the same wrong angle
